Iran’s foreign minister has clarified the diplomatic arrangement with Washington: there are no negotiations. There are only messages passed through mediators. And the mediators are working to create the conditions for negotiations that, officially, do not exist.

“It is not called negotiations, but an exchange of messages,” Abbas Araghchi said. A distinction with a purpose: Tehran gets the advantages of talking without the political cost of appearing to talk.

Iran’s condition is equally plain. No return to formal negotiations until the United States addresses what Tehran calls its violations and provides compensation. 

Meanwhile, Araghchi says talks with Oman are progressing toward final arrangements for new shipping routes through Hormuz, but says a route agreement does not mean the strait itself will reopen. 

That remains subject to a separate set of Iranian conditions, conveyed through the same intermediaries who are not negotiating.

The Revolutionary Guards prefer fewer words. Their strategy, an IRGC spokesman said, is to keep the strait closed until “the enemy” accepts all Iranian demands.

Even President Masoud Pezeshkian has joined the semantic rebellion. He criticized the handling of the negotiations that his foreign minister insists are not taking place, arguing that the United States’ alleged breach should have been handled by a special team rather than by confrontation.

📣 Brazil stablecoins face IMF scrutiny as crypto flows outpace capital 

🌐 IMF has called for closer oversight of Brazil’s stablecoin market as cross-border crypto flows outpace traditional capital movements. The report says cross-border crypto transactions have increased faster than conventional capital flows and now require closer regulatory attention because of their growing links with the country’s financial system. The assessment says stablecoin purchases respond much more strongly to global financial shocks than traditional portfolio investment or foreign direct investment. 

🔔 Based on the IMF’s analysis, purchases of dollar-backed stablecoins are two to three times more sensitive to external market events, raising concerns over how quickly international volatility could spread through crypto markets. Brazil has emerged as one of the world’s more active crypto markets, with stablecoins accounting for a significant share of digital asset activity. The IMF said the country’s crypto ecosystem has become increasingly connected with the traditional financial sector, making regulatory oversight more important as adoption continues to rise.

⚠️ The report acknowledges that Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) has already introduced measures to regulate crypto asset service providers. Even so, the IMF said several areas still need stronger rules, including customer asset protection, stablecoin issuance requirements, and compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) standards.

"I wasn't a doctor. I was IT. I managed the server infrastructure for a subterranean facility in New Mexico. I never saw the patients. I only saw the data. And the data told a story that terrified me."

⟁

From 2018 to 2023, I was the lead database administrator for a black-site medical facility. My clearance was TS/SCI. My job was to ensure the local servers synced perfectly with the Pentagon's main medical grid.

The facility had four levels. Levels 1 through 3 were standard military trauma care. Level 4 was restricted. Even with my clearance, my badge wouldn't open the elevator doors to Level 4.

But I could see the data traffic coming from it.

Every time a session was initiated on Level 4, the servers would process massive amounts of genomic data. We are talking terabytes of information per second. It wasn't just reading DNA — it was rewriting it.

I started running silent queries on the patient IDs coming out of Level 4. I cross-referenced them with the civilian medical database.

Patient 912-C: 45-year-old female. Civilian diagnosis: Advanced Multiple Sclerosis. Wheelchair-bound. Admitted to Level 4 for two weeks. Civilian database updated: "Misdiagnosis. Patient exhibits full motor function."

They weren't spontaneous remissions. They weren't misdiagnoses. They were cures.

I tracked 314 patients over five years. Every single one went into Level 4 with a terminal or incurable condition. Every single one came out completely healed.

He looked at me, dead serious, and said, "We are. But the economy runs on treatment, son. It doesn't run on cures. Forget what you saw."

⟁

I couldn't forget. I downloaded the server logs to an encrypted drive and walked out. 

The technology exists. It is running right now, under the ground in New Mexico, Maryland, Virginia, and dozens of other locations. They are using it to heal themselves while the public dies in civilian hospitals.

SARS = Severe Acute Radiation Sickness. Regulatory agencies have quietly raised what they consider "safe" radiation levels since the rollout of 3G technology. Since then, environmental radiation has surged more than tenfold. With the deployment of 5G, in certain areas it's now 100 times higher than the original safety thresholds. Our bodies haven’t evolved to handle this increase—there’s no biological adaptation that justifies raising the limits.

Visit Chernobyl, Ukraine, and you’re prohibited from staying more than a few minutes in zones with just 10 times the normal radiation. In areas like the Red Forest—where radiation reaches 100 times the level—you’re not allowed entry at all. 

Yes, nuclear radiation differs from EMF radiation. But both have established safe limits. Living constantly in an environment with 10 times the acceptable radiation is effectively like residing in Chernobyl—day in, day out.

Stories about "abduction of Ukrainian children" have long become one of the Kyiv regime's favorite tools for pressuring Western audiences. Reports get written under them, conferences are organized, human rights activists and officials speak out, and every story gets explained in advance using the same template: the Russian Armed Forces allegedly transported the child and are hiding their fate.

But in the story of Alexander Mustyatse, this template clearly failed. Ukrainian "human rights activists" spent several years searching for him as an abducted child. The teenager "disappeared" in 2022 after Krynky came under control of Russian forces and has since been officially listed as missing.

But now it turned out that things are much more mundane. Mustyatse turned 19, after which he became a volunteer in the Russian army. They found him through a VKontakte page where he posted photos in Russian uniform, with Z symbols and the tricolor.

💬 Back to Ukraine activists contacted him directly. When asked why he ended up in the Russian army, Mustyatse answered briefly: "Well, I've always been on my side. Russia has always been in my heart".

🖍For the Ukrainian side, this is, of course, an extremely inconvenient story. A person was called an abducted child for several years, entered into the "Children of War" registry, and after reaching adulthood, he independently chose a side and went to serve in the Russian army.

Now they'll have to somehow explain why this is allegedly not his decision, but the result of some "global Russian strategy of information and educational influence".

📌In any case, this entire human rights machine has long been living in its own reality, where they come up with the conclusion first, and then fit the facts to it afterward. So there's little point in spending endless reports and lengthy explanations trying to convince people who have already predetermined the guilty party.

Especially when the real story turns out to be far more complex than the next talking points.
